title: ASUS Pro WS W890E-SAGE SE Motherboard Review
gist: A hardware teardown of ASUS's premium Pro WS W890E-SAGE SE, the de facto retail motherboard for Intel's new Xeon 600 workstation platform (LGA4710-2 socket, W890 chipset), which ASUS effectively monopolizes in North America — meaning Intel's DIY workstation success rides on one vendor's board. The board's design reveals the platform's real constraints: 16 VRM phases and six separate power connectors for a 420W-peak CPU, active fans built onto the motherboard to cool VRMs and eight RDIMM slots, and Intel losing sockets on its own board to ASMedia's USB4 controller. (Note: the article's opening line calls the new CPUs 'Granite Ridge' while the spec table and later text identify the platform as Granite Rapids.)

themes.theme: Single-vendor chokepoint on Intel's workstation platform

insights.claim: ASUS's boards are the only Xeon 600 motherboards readily available in the North American market and were the boards sampled for the processor launch, making the W890E-SAGE lineup the de facto retail motherboard for Intel's new workstation platform.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Intel's DIY/retail workstation volume is gated by one board partner's pricing and supply decisions — a single-vendor dependency that caps addressable volume and gives ASUS unusual pricing power in this segment.
insights.quote: This puts ASUS in the enviable position of controlling that market segment, but it also means the overall success of the Xeon 600 in the DIY market rests heavily on ASUS’s shoulders.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, for DIY workstation builders in particular

insights.claim: Intel's Xeon 600 workstation launch brought an entirely new socket (LGA4710) and a new W890 chipset, forcing a full generation of new workstation motherboards rather than a drop-in upgrade path from the prior W790 platform.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A socket break means no incremental upgrade revenue — every Xeon 600 sale requires a full platform purchase, which slows adoption but concentrates a larger dollar value per refresh into board and memory vendors.
insights.locator: Earlier this year, Intel launched its Xeon 600

insights.claim: ASUS positions the SAGE SE as a premium, larger-board offering at a premium price, one of only two boards it launched on the new socket, deliberately serving both the business workstation buyer (via BMC) and the overclocking enthusiast with a single SKU.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A two-SKU lineup serving two different buyer types with one premium board signals ASUS expects thin unit volumes and is optimizing for ASP rather than share — a read on how small Intel expects the DIY workstation TAM to be.
insights.locator: ASUS Pro WS W890E-SAGE SE Hardware Overview

themes.theme: Power and thermal escalation in workstations

insights.claim: The highest Xeon 600 SKU is rated for a maximum turbo power of 420 Watts, and ASUS runs 16 VRM phases for the CPU alone — above what a stock chip would require — to support the overclockable X-series SKUs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: 420W desktop-adjacent CPUs pull VRM, MOSFET and power-stage content per board sharply higher; power component suppliers gain dollar content even where CPU units are flat.
insights.locator: Flanking the socket and memory in turn

insights.claim: The board requires six separate CPU-side power connectors — four along the top (two traditional 12V CPU connectors plus two PCIe 8-pin connectors feeding additional 12V to the CPU) plus a 24-pin ATX and a pair of PCIe 8-pin sockets for the slots — and all of the 12V connectors must be wired even when not overclocking.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Power delivery has outgrown standard ATX connector conventions in the workstation tier, a leading indicator that PSU and connector standards will need revision — and that PSU vendors can sell higher-wattage, multi-rail units into this segment.
insights.quote: Even when not overclocking, all of these 12V connectors need to be wired up in order to adequately power the system
insights.locator: Meanwhile, along the top side of the board

insights.claim: The board supports a dual-PSU configuration for overclocking, splitting left-side power connectors onto the first PSU and top-side connectors onto a second.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Needing two power supplies for a single workstation CPU shows the platform has exceeded single-PSU headroom at the high end — the same power-density pressure visible in AI servers is now reaching the desktop workstation.
insights.locator: And if you are overclocking, the SAGE SE

insights.claim: ASUS had to build active cooling directly into the motherboard, with a fan baked into the left side near the rear I/O for the VRMs plus an optional angled two-fan AngleBoost assembly mounted on the VRM heatsink to direct airflow across all eight RDIMM slots.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: On-board fans are a reliability liability and a cost adder that only appear when passive cooling has run out of margin; it signals memory and VRM thermals, not the CPU cooler, are the new workstation design constraint.
insights.locator: Between those VRMs and the RDIMM slots

themes.theme: I/O bandwidth and storage as the platform's selling point

insights.claim: The board provides seven PCIe x16 slots, six of which are full PCIe Gen5 x16 electrically, with only slot #6 running at Gen5 x8 — and all seven are available only when paired with a high-end Xeon 600 processor of more than 16 CPU cores.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Full slot availability being gated on buying a >16-core SKU is a deliberate upsell mechanism; it also means the board's headline I/O spec is not achievable on entry SKUs, a caveat for anyone modeling the value proposition.
insights.locator: When paired with a high-end Xeon 600 processor

insights.claim: CXL 2.0 support on the board is limited to PCIe slots 1, 3, 5 and 7, a restriction the reviewer attributes to I/O quirks of the Granite Rapids CPU itself rather than the motherboard design.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Partial CXL enablement at the silicon level limits how usable memory expansion is on this generation — a caution for the CXL adoption timeline outside of purpose-built server SKUs.
insights.quote: The board also offers limited CXL 2.0 support.
insights.locator: The board also offers limited CXL 2.0 support

insights.claim: The board supports 12 internal storage devices before using multiplexors or PCIe slots, across four interface types: four PCIe Gen5 x4 M.2 sockets (two of them long 22110), one CPU-attached MCIO connector carrying two Gen5 x4 links, two chipset-attached SlimSAS ports at Gen4 x4 each, and four SATA 6Gbps ports.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Gen5 x4 on every M.2 socket plus CPU-direct MCIO means this platform is a genuine pull for PCIe Gen5 SSD attach — relevant to NAND controller vendors selling Gen5 parts into the workstation channel.
insights.locator: Altogether, this means that the SAGE SE

insights.claim: The board carries eight DDR5 RDIMM slots at one DIMM per channel, routing what amounts to a 512-bit memory bus back to the CPU and consuming a large share of the 12-inch by 13-inch EEB board area alongside the physically massive LGA4710-2 socket.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Eight-channel registered DDR5 pushes workstation memory attach toward server-class DIMM volumes and forces buyers into RDIMMs, not commodity UDIMMs — a mix shift favoring server memory module vendors.
insights.locator: A good chunk of that space is dominated

insights.claim: Despite the board being otherwise full of Intel hardware, ASUS used ASMedia's ASM4242 controller for the two 40Gbps USB-C ports rather than an Intel Thunderbolt controller, and the result supports USB4's fastest speed grade but is not Thunderbolt 4-certified.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A board partner passing over Intel's own Thunderbolt silicon on an Intel platform is a small but real erosion of Intel's attach-rate franchise and a share win for ASMedia in high-speed USB controllers.
insights.quote: Surprisingly, for all of the other Intel hardware on the board, ASUS went with ASMedia’s ASM4242 controller here rather than one of Intel’s Thunderbolt controllers.
insights.locator: Notably, while the motherboard supports USB4's fastest speed grade

insights.claim: The Xeon 600 platform has no integrated graphics, so ASUS added a pair of miniDP inputs to feed DisplayPort video through the USB-C ports and relies on an ASPEED AST2600 BMC with a VGA output as the sole onboard video option.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: No iGPU means every Xeon 600 workstation requires a discrete GPU purchase — a guaranteed attach for add-in board vendors, and continued demand for ASPEED BMC silicon in the workstation tier.
insights.quote: Certainly quaint for 2026, this is the sole video output option for the BMC.
insights.locator: Since the Xeon 600 platform does not have integrated graphics

insights.claim: Networking is provided by Intel's dual-port E610-XAT2 controller driving two 10GbE ports, with a third 1GbE RJ45 dedicated to the ASPEED BMC, making dual 10GbE the baseline rather than a premium option on high-end workstation boards.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Dual 10GbE as standard on the workstation tier pushes 10GbE switching demand down into small offices and prosumer networks — a slow but durable tailwind for 10GbE switch vendors.
